newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania govt mulls 1997 budget changes to woo IMF.
newsitem.headline: Romania govt mulls 1997 budget changes to woo IMF.

text.p: Romania's government, keen to impress a IMF delegation considering further loan tranches, on Monday examined a revised 1997 state budget in a bid to meet key economic targets.
The revision has been expected for months since price liberalisation forced inflation far higher than initially predicted. But no details of changes were made public.
"There is no risk of exceeding our budget gap," Industry Minister Calin Popescu Tariceanu told reporters after meeting the International Monetary Fund team.
"You can be sure some budgetary items will be reduced following lower returns from revenues."

Finance Minister Ciumara blames low revenues on a slow start to ambitious plan to speed up privatisation and shut down inefficient factories and farms. Revenue from sell-offs in June, he said, was modest at ten billion lei ($945,000).
But government ministers made plain they would defend their budget allocations against plans for cutbacks to meet IMF deficit targets.

Under a reform programme approved by the IMF and backed by credits of $430 million, the centrist government promised to deliver an austere budget. That meant cutting the consolidated budget deficit to 4.5 percent of gross domestic product this year from about 5.8 percent in 1996.
The consolidated budget includes state budget, local government budgets, the social security budget and various extra-budgetary funds.
The IMF team, in Bucharest for two weeks, has declined comment on whether it will recommend releasing the second of five $86 million loan disbursements in the coming months.

The reform programme, aimed at speeding up the slow pace of change under the government's leftist predecessor, aims at lower inflation, a stable currency, cautious budget spending and faster privatisation and restructuring.
The budget's original inflation target of 90 percent for 1997 was put beyond reach by unexpected price jumps which hit a record 30 percent in March alone.
That has since been adjusted to an annual figure of 110-120 percent, but most economists say a figure of 150 percent is more realistic, with price rises of 101.2 percent recorded since December.
The budget cuts are in part intended to fulfil pledges in last year's election campaign to ease income and profit taxes -- now at up to 60 percent and 38 percent respectively.
Media reports ahead of Monday's meeting suggested that Finance Minister Mircea Ciumara would snub a campaign by the country's hard-pressed Health Ministry to seek more funds.
Health Minister Stefan Dragulescu told reporters on Monday he would proceed with his plan to seek a bigger allocation.
"The government has to understand that health is a national priority," he said.

The ministry has come under fire for the low salaries paid to doctors and other medical staff and a shortfall in revenue. It has already announced plans to phase out subsidies for prescription and make patients pay for medicine in full.
